sections.text: ## The Editor's Principle

metadata.title: Graphic Design - Landscape and Taxonomy

sections.text:
| Situation | Approach | Why |
|-----------|----------|-----|
| Information clarity under space constraints | Swiss grid system (modular grid + single typeface) | Constraint-driven layout maximizes legibility and consistency |
| Brand identity needing confident singular vision | American-modernist single-solution approach (Rand model) | One definitive mark, presented with conviction; scales across all touchpoints |
| Multi-language or international audience | Swiss style (Akzidenz-Grotesk/Helvetica, asymmetric grid) | Neutral typography; visual hierarchy doesn't depend on reading the language |
| Expressive, cultural, or editorial design | Post-Swiss (Weingart, Carson, Brody) or historical reference | Break the grid when the content demands emotional response over clarity |
| Systematic corporate identity program | Standards manual approach (1960s tradition) | Define every application so consistency survives delegation to non-designers |
| Digital/interactive design system | Component-based design system (Atomic Design model) | Reusable components compose like software modules; consistency at scale |

sections.text: # Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   THE BAUHAUS (1919-1933)                     |
|                                                               |
|  WEIMAR 1919-1925   DESSAU 1925-1932   BERLIN 1932-1933       |
|  (Gropius)          (Gropius -> Meyer  (Mies van der Rohe)    |
|                      -> Mies)                                 |
|                                                               |
|  THESIS: Unify fine art, craft, and industrial production     |
|  under a single educational and aesthetic framework           |
|                                                               |
|  CLOSED: Nazis declared it degenerate / communist             |
|  DIASPORA: Staff scattered to USA -> shaped American design   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
               |
               v
+-----------------------------------------------+
|  LEGACY CHANNELS                              |
|                                               |
|  -> Art education (Foundation Course model)   |
|  -> Corporate identity (IBM, etc.)            |
|  -> Architecture (International Style)        |
|  -> Typography (geometric sans-serifs)        |
|  -> Industrial design (form follows function) |
+-----------------------------------------------+
```

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: ## What Made the Bauhaus Different

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
Before the Bauhaus, European art education split along two tracks:
- **Fine arts academies**: painting, sculpture, "pure" art
- **Technical schools**: applied craft, trades

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
The Bauhaus declared this split false and damaging. Gropius's founding manifesto
(1919) opened: "The ultimate aim of all creative activity is building!"

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
Designer =/= Craftsman         Designer = Craftsman = Thinker
```

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: ## The School Structure

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: Every student at the Bauhaus took the same path:

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  VORKURS (Foundation Course)                     |
|  6 months                                        |
|  Taught by: Itten, then Moholy-Nagy, Albers      |
|  Content: Color theory, materials, basic forms   |
|  Purpose: Unlearn academic habits                |
+--------------------------------------------------+
                    |
                    v
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  WORKSHOPS (3 years)                             |
|                                                  |
|  Two masters per workshop:                       |
|  MASTER OF FORM (artist) + MASTER OF CRAFT       |
|                                                  |
|  Workshops:                                      |
|  - Typography / Printing                         |
|  - Weaving                                       |
|  - Metal / Furniture                             |
|  - Ceramics (Weimar only)                        |
|  - Wall Painting                                 |
|  - Theater                                       |
|  - Photography (added 1929)                      |
+--------------------------------------------------+
                    |
                    v
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  BUILDING WORKSHOP (advanced)                    |
|  Architecture + comprehensive design             |
|  Gropius's ultimate goal (arrived late)          |
+--------------------------------------------------+
```

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
The dual-master model was key: a practicing artist taught concept, a practicing
craftsman taught technique. Neither alone was sufficient.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: ## The Aesthetic Output

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
Bayer's "universal" typeface (1925) was geometric, lowercase-first, functionalist.
The Bauhaus questioned the necessity of capital letters as aesthetically arbitrary.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
BAUHAUS TYPOGRAPHY PRINCIPLES
------------------------------
- Geometric construction (circle, square, triangle as basis)
- Sans-serif favored (no historical ornament)
- Grid alignment
- Red + black two-color printing (Soviet-influenced)
- Text + image as unified design field

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
DESIGN OBJECT         DESIGNER          YEAR   SIGNIFICANCE
-----------------     --------          ----   -----------
Wassily Chair         Marcel Breuer     1925   First tubular steel furniture
Cesca Chair (B32)     Marcel Breuer     1928   Cantilever; still in production
MT 49 Tea Infuser     Marianne Brandt   1924   Machine-aesthetic metal craft
MT 8 Desk Lamp        Wilhelm Wagenfeld 1924   "Bauhaus lamp"; still produced
Nesting Tables        Marcel Breuer     1926   Modular design principle
Weaving              Gunta Stolzl      1920s  Elevated textiles to art
```

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: ## The Three Phases and Their Shift

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
DESSAU (1925-1932)
  Tone: Rationalist, industrial, proto-corporate
  New building designed by Gropius himself
  Moholy-Nagy's machine aesthetic takes hold
  Bayer's typography; steel furniture
  Output: Industrial prototypes, mass-producible forms

sections.text: ## The Diaspora: Bauhaus in America

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
1933: Bauhaus closes
      |
      v
+------------------------------------------+
|  STAFF AND STUDENTS FLEE EUROPE          |
|                                          |
|  Moholy-Nagy -> Chicago (New Bauhaus,    |
|                  1937 = Institute of     |
|                  Design)                 |
|                                          |
|  Gropius -> Harvard Graduate School      |
|             of Design (chair, 1937)      |
|                                          |
|  Mies van der Rohe -> IIT Chicago        |
|             (Architecture dept, 1938)    |
|                                          |
|  Josef Albers -> Black Mountain College, |
|             then Yale (1950)             |
|                                          |
|  Herbert Bayer -> NYC advertising /      |
|             Aspen Institute              |
+------------------------------------------+
      |
      v
American design education transforms:
- Foundation courses become standard
- Functional modernism becomes corporate house style
- IBM, CBS, Container Corp hire Bauhaus-trained designers
```

sections.text: ## The Political Dimension

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text: The Bauhaus was caught in Weimar-era politics throughout:

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
```
TENSION                           RESOLUTION
-------                           ----------
Art for art vs art for society    Never resolved; Gropius vs Meyer
Socialist collective vs market    School sold designs; industrialist patrons
German nationalism vs             Always suspect; Dessau city council
internationalism                  tried to cut funding repeatedly
"Degenerate art" accusation       Nazis targeted Kandinsky, Klee specifically
```

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
Hannes Meyer (director 1928-1930) was a committed Marxist who pushed the school
explicitly toward social housing design. Gropius's letters show tension; Mies
depoliticized the school again but too late.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
The Bauhaus is present in every:
- Sans-serif UI font (Helvetica's spiritual ancestors were geometric sans)
- Grid-based web layout (the grid as universal structure)
- Design system thinking (systematic visual language)
- Industrial product designed for mass production
- Foundation course at any art/design school worldwide

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
The distinction between a graphic designer and "someone who makes things look
nice" is a Bauhaus-derived distinction: design is disciplined problem-solving
using visual means.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
- [Graphic Design Overview](00-OVERVIEW.md) places Bauhaus inside the broader design discipline.
- [Swiss Style](02-SWISS-STYLE.md) follows Bauhaus rationalism into grid-based international typography.
- [Grid Systems](04-GRID-SYSTEMS.md) turns Bauhaus composition principles into repeatable layout architecture.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
**"Bauhaus was a style"** -- It was first a pedagogy and thesis. The aesthetic
(geometric, sans-serif, primary colors) emerged from the ideas, not the other
way around. Many Bauhaus teachers (Klee, Kandinsky) made highly personal work.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
**"Bauhaus = minimalism"** -- No. The school was interested in color, theater,
weaving, photography, ceramics. Mies van der Rohe's phase was minimal; the
overall school was not. "Less is more" was Mies's position.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
**"Bauhaus = German"** -- Yes in origin, but the output was explicitly
internationalist. That was part of what made it suspect to nationalists.

metadata.title: Bauhaus: Total Design and the School

sections.text:
**"The Foundation Course is just art class"** -- Itten's and Albers's foundation
courses were systematic investigations of perception, materials, and form. Albers's
"Interaction of Color" is still a reference text for anyone doing visual work.
